segments.description: On screen: The image shows a man standing in front of a screen displaying a sports event. He appears to be giving a presentation or speaking at an event related to tennis, as indicated by the presence of a tennis racket on the screen and the text "COACHES' CONFERENCE" visible on the screen. The man is wearing a dark shirt with a logo on it, which could suggest he is associated with a particular organization or team. There are no visible numbers or specific measurements in this image.

Hi, coaches. It is a privilege to introduce Michael Boll. Michael represented Australia as a swimmer from 1979 to 1985 and as a coach from 1991 to 2021. He is a five-time Olympic swimming coach, having coached eight individual Olympic medalists, including Stephanie Rice and Australia's most decorated Olympic athlete, Emma McKeon. Michael is sharing his insights into developing positive culture for high performance. Welcome Michael. So Michael, welcome today. Thanks for doing this and sharing your insights with the tennis Australia coach members and tennis coaches from around the world. Because we are a tennis coaching community, can you just share some light on your career and transition from a swimmer and an athlete to your coaching profession now? Well, it goes back a long way, Jay. I've been coaching for about 34 years. Started out at the University of Queensland at St Lucia. I coached there for a couple of years, then moved across to St Peter's for a very short amount of time, maybe six months or nine months. Then across to Centenary Pool for about 12 months. Then swimming Queensland offered me a job as State Coaching Director in 1991. I was in that role through to 2002, so for about 11 years. And that job involved going around the State of Queensland doing coach accreditation courses and doing development squad days for young up-and-coming swimmers. As well as doing that, I was coaching a squad full-time.

So I was very, very busy during that period of time. Then I moved across to St Peter's in 2003. I was there for 14 years as the head coach of that program there. And we really started out with nothing and built that club into the number one club in Australia. Dean Boxall, who's the coach of Ariane Titmus, was one of the assistant coaches I had. He's now currently the head coach of that program. And then in 2017, in September, I moved across to Griffith University. And in the last two weeks, I've moved again through to Southport Aquatic Centre. So I've been here for two weeks. So a bit of an interesting career, I suppose. I was swimming from the time I was about eight, up until probably 23, 24 years of age, and started coaching at about 25 years of age. And so in that time, you've seen a lot of changes within swimming. We look back at the 80s and the rocky and turbulent times, the East German fiasco, moving into some real ups and downs throughout Australian swimming. You've experienced them all. What do you see as the main drivers in reaching those peaks, the better performances from the Australian teams? Well, I think it's really targeted programs. I think Greg Lawler, who was the chairman of Queensland swimming for over 30 years, he did a really good job. Queensland never used to be the dominant state that it is now. New South Wales was the dominant state. And Greg Lawler amassed a group of about three or four coaches,

Laurie Lawrence, Ken Wood, Joe King, those sorts of calibre coaches who are probably the best in their field at the time, got them together when Queensland was on the ropes and came up with what they called the Target Squad Program. So Queensland Target Squad, and it was targeting Olympic success. So they formed a program. Swimming Queensland ran it for about 20 years, and then the Queensland Academy of Sport saw it was very, very successful. And the last 15 to 20 years, they've taken over the Target Squad Program. So I think initially it was that Greg Lawler really giving it legs, he really got the coaches together as a group and got the swimmers together as a group, and it started out purely in simply those good swimmers and those good coaches coming together for Friday, Saturday, Sunday and doing training sessions together. That morphed into them getting funding where they were able to get sponsors and overseas travel, so competitions and camps, and then it just morphed into what it is today. It's a multi-million dollar program. So it started out back in the 1980s, and it's morphed into probably one of the world-leading programs in the year 2021. Prior to the Target Squad being developed, would you say that the coaches were almost isolationists and that they tried to keep separate from each other, whereas now it seems to be more collaborative in their approaches? I think definitely.

Back in the 70s, the coaches wanted to punch each other. It wasn't particularly harmonious. I think there were a lot of petty jealousies and everything else, but I think some of the really good coaches that we had back in the 80s, the John Carews, the Bill Sweetenham's, the Laurie Lawrence's and those guys really worked out that working together as a group made Queensland better and it made us all as individuals better. So I think a lot of information sharing amongst the coaches, swimmers from the top programs around Brisbane coming together for those three-day training camps was a great way of fast-tracking coach development and also athlete development. In those camps and subsequent camps that are running as well, what did you see the benefits and the outcomes from those camps? Well, if I could use the example on coaching Emma McKean at the moment who just came back from a very successful Olympic campaign in Tokyo and we transitioned her into a sprint swimmer and she's been involved in the national event camp program for the last seven or eight years where all the best sprinters come together for a week's training, all the best middle-distance swimmers, all the best distance swimmers, the best butterflies, backstrikers, breast-strikers, etc. All get together. We stay in the same hotel, but because there's so many people all the eight best female butterflies, the eight best male butterflies

all go to a training venue and they train together. So Emma has been a party of that for the last eight years and going along and watching Kate Campbell and Bronte Campbell watching what their training standard was like. I guess it's a light bulb moment for young developing swimmers. They're able to see very clearly what the best of the best are doing on a day-to-day basis in training and it just sets that standard that's a little bit higher. We thought pushing 27 for 50 freestyle was really good until we saw the Campbell girls pushing 26s and now they're pushing 25. I think the swimmers seeing what other people are doing and the coaches seeing what the very best athletes are doing really teaches everyone what world class is. That's what I've taken away from the national event camps and I know that Emma has taken that same mindset away from those week camps that we have. So for the athletes themselves what do they get from it? Do they recognise those benchmarks? How do you improve their motivation? I just think it gives them direction. I think when you're working as a silo when you're a big fish in a small pond, when you get to the big pond you don't know what the standard is but by the top 800 metre freestyle women getting together and in the top eight women we've got three of the top eight in the world in the 100 freestyle having those swimmers come together for a week long training camp

so they're able to see the standard and they take that standard away. It's no good being at that standard for one week out of 52. You've got to be consistently with the training blocks that you're putting together you're trying to consistently emulate the standard that the top swimmers were showing on that week. I think having the information is one thing but now backing up and using that information to lift your standard higher is probably the working piece that everyone needs to take away from it. So collaboration of those camps with the coaches, what are your conversations around it? Well I think it's getting experience from people that have been there for a long time. I try and learn from coaches that have not been there as a flash in the pan but coaches that have been producing and have got that sustainable success that they've had year upon year upon year. So for example in swimming for us it's the Dennis Cottrells and those sorts of people that have been on the national team for 30 plus years and have had continued success at the Olympic level. They're the people that I try and learn from. So what we do during the week long of the camp, we're not only getting together at the pool but we're discussing training sets and sessions that we're doing in our home program. So when we get together at night and we sit around and have a couple of beers and have a meal, the coaches that is not the athletes

we're there in a learning, it's not really a structured learning format but I think it's where you learn the most because you're asking questions to the people that are your mentors, you're asking questions of them that you've got interest in. So we're lucky in swimming to have a lot of coaches that have been on the scene for a long time and I guess they're the mentors that we try and learn from. Along with your success from your athletes in the pool you mentioned Dino before but also Nick, you've had two assistant coaches who've gone on to the Olympic coaches. What do you attribute, do you take that philosophy from the camps back into your own training environments? Yeah well I think I had the good fortune of working I guess to answer your question, thinking back the first six years I was at St Peter's I had Mick Palfrey working as my assistant coach and for the last six years I had Dean Boxall working as my assistant coach and right from the outset when I was at St Peter's I believe in trying to inservice the coaches that you've got working with you and your organisation so you're all on the same page and I think one of the mantras that I tried to set with the coaching staff that we had that every program in Australia would look up to us at St Peter's as being Australian and world leading so what I told our coaches at our monthly meetings was that the expectation from my part as the head coach

of this program is that if there are two St Peter's swimmers in the final at national championships we want the other six programs to know that they're in for a hell of a fight. We want the reputation as being hard, tough talented, exceptional at what we did so that was the mindset that they filtered down to their respective groups so the junior coach the intermediate coach and the senior coach were all that same sort of mindset so I was very big on trying to instill in my coaches the need to keep our reputation as a club up very very high so what I tried to do was I tried to have monthly meetings with the head coaches of those respective programs in our organisation so the junior coach and our definition of junior coach was 12 and under, our intermediate coach the definition was 12 to 17 years and then I was the senior coach 18 years and older so we get together once a month over Brecci and we just sort out and I'd answer questions where I could for all the coaches that were working in that program so we had about 12 coaches working I didn't ask all of them to come along it was just the head coaches I think when you involve too many people in that sort of discussion it gets too filtered so it was just the head junior coach, the head intermediate coach and myself would get together over Brecci and we'd just discuss any problems that they were having or if they had any questions they wanted to

ask that was it. I was a firm believer in those coaches that were responsible for those groups sorting out any problems they had within their group because I think it was part of their development. It's no good me coming in to the junior program and sorting out his problems or her problems for her I believe in empowering the coaches to look after their own problems and if there was no resolution then I'd try and come in. If it was an argument between the parent and the coach or other swimmers within the squad were having disagreements or whatever I'd try and let those coaches sort out their problems but if we didn't get resolutions then I'd try and come in and just talk my way through it with them because I think what I saw as my job is to help mentor these coaches because one day they're going to be the head coach of a different program and Mick Palfrey who was the intermediate coach when I first came to St Peter's after about six years he moved over to Western Australia where he was the head coach of the WACE program over there so I think the skills that he learned while he was at St Peter's and all the problems that ensued with parents, with staff, with athletes he was able to conflict-resolute really well within that confines of his group and that gave him the skills to go on one day and become the head coach of the WACE program, Western Australian Institute of Sport program

Do you see bits of yourself in their coaching? I think you do. I think my mantra on coaching is you're trying to create an environment that's positive and hard working. I think you need harmony within the group so it's important the relationships, inter-squad relationships are good. That's sacrosanct to me. We don't want to have people fighting within the group because it creates disunity distrust all those things that you don't want within your environment are there if you've got people that aren't on the same page. Whenever we have problems I try and sit the athletes down and I just tell them we haven't got to be best friends that is the athletes but we're together for at least 5 hours every day and we all want a harmonious workplace environment so it's making sure that we're making allowances for each other and there's nothing worse than being in an environment where you've got that continual bickering between one athlete and another. If that happens I sit them down, I try and resolve it and if I see it continuing I sit them down again and I say if we can't sort this out one of you is going to both. It's come down to that a couple of times and it's always worked itself out because most of the kids didn't want to leave the program so they were able to make the adjustments to be able to work in the confines of the group effectively. So within your group you recognise as having what's probably

the best program in the country if not one of the best programs in the world what do you put it down to? You talk about the unity in the group and the culture that you've created. What's the secret source behind it? Well I think you as a coach number one thing to me is communication. Like I think having that relationship with the athlete like they've got to understand and they've got to believe that you've got their back covered whether it's not just with sport but with life. So part of your role is to help them become better people. So that's a big thing for me they've got to understand that I've got their welfare covered as a human being even first and foremost before them as an athlete. So I think having that workplace environment that's positive and hard working I think it's just infectious so I think when you've got people who are hard working and achieving I think it just sets a great standard for everyone that comes in. We've got a little pyramid that we share with everyone in the group as well. There's a very good basketball coach called John Wooden from America. They won eight or nine NCAA championships at UCLA back in the 1970s and 1980s and John Wooden was the coach and he created this pyramid of success and they're all little blocks that he believes are important to the success of your organization. And when he speaks about it the two corner blocks which he believes are the ones that hold

the pyramid up on the left corner is a word he uses is industriousness and the word on the right hand corner the right hand block is enthusiasm. And he deems industriousness as being the coach and the athlete understanding that to be successful you've got to work hard. So we as coaches and your athletes as athletes have to understand to get better they've got to work bloody hard and enthusiasm that right corner you've got to walk into the pool environment or the tennis court positive and happy to be there not walking through the front door kicking stones as you're walking in and not being happy about being there. And I think I make them all say good morning or good afternoon when they come in and make sure they say good bye to their teammates as they're leaving. I think it's important that they've got that respect for the coaches that are within the press, not just me but it's all the coaches, the strength and conditioning, the sport signers, the biomechanists everyone that's working with our program I make sure that there's a respect for all those people that are trying to help make them better. And I think that's just infectious when you've got the best athletes who are achieving high we've got five Olympic individual medalists within the program now. When you've got those people coming in that have got a great work ethic that are very respectful and the people that are below them

understand that that's the behaviour that you know we're accepting nothing, well it can be more but nothing less than that behaviour is what we expect. I had the opportunity to come in and watch the you delivering one session a couple of weeks ago and you had Mack Horton the Rio Olympic gold medalist from the 400 Free and he was doing a set of broken 400s and it was his last couple coming down and everyone had stopped to watch but also to cheer him on so that he would produce his best effort. Is that something how do you foster that environment? Well I think it's just those words I said before like you're trying to create a positive hard working environment. So when you've got athletes supporting other athletes I think that's just it's almost like osmosis. You have two or three people supporting then tomorrow there'll be five or six or even more supporting. So I think it's just something that's self perpetuating you know you get a couple of people doing it then you'll have more and more doing it tomorrow. So I think you as a coach have got to set that standard like I'll sometimes say guys so and so is on their last effort here you finished your set let's come over and cheer them on and then what you find happening next week is they'll see what's going on and they'll do it themselves. So you try and set that behaviour up but in the end you haven't got to do it it's the athletes taking

ownership of themselves. So I think you know the more that you try and engender that over time it might take a week it might take a month you'll find that they'll do it themselves over time. So it's just you're going to try and create that dynamic within the group that you've got. It's not an easy thing to do but I think if you have an active participant as in the athletes that you've got wanting to do it then I think it's sort of self perpetuating. But we've got people within our group that are fighting each other for spots on the team but they're just a supporter of what they are for their team mate. So I think you know Cody Simpson has just started up in the last 12 months with us and Bowen Goff both butterflies both trying to get on the world championship team in 12 weeks time but they're nothing but support for each other. They'll finish a set off and they'll punch Fisk after it saying you know great job great job and one day Bowen will win the next day Cody will win but they've got that same commitment to each other at the Fisk pump after the set so it's nice that they're pushing each other and working together as a group. I think you'll always get a better athlete output out of your athletes when they're supporting one another like that. You've had some amazing athletes Steph Rice, Evan McKinn personality wise they're completely different. How do you manage that? I think you just don't try and change them too much

I think what I've learnt with success over a period of time there's no pigeon hole as to what success looks like. I think it's them trying to be a better version of themselves. So Stephanie Rice is very outgoing, very gregarious, very confident, self-assured everything else. She's an Olympic gold medalist. Evan McKinn is an Olympic gold medalist she's the total antithesis of that. She's reserved, she's quiet, doesn't like bringing attention to herself and she's very successful. So I don't make Stephanie like that and I don't make Emma like that. I think you've just got to celebrate what they are as people and don't change them. So it's really keeping their natural personality intact and letting them be themselves. And the only thing I'm really interested in is just their level that they can work at obviously to be successful where they are at last season is ancient history. They've got to lift the standard of what they're doing if they want to improve and it's really just about continuing to improve you know. I think as a coach I've got to keep improving and the athletes have to keep improving whether they've broken a wall record or whether they've failed last season. They've got to be looking at improving if they want to be successful next season. How do you go about self-improvement? I think talking to other coaches. I mean Tokyo was only six months ago. I've forgotten about

what happened there now and I was only talking about it to someone this morning. I'm fixated on Paris now. It's two and a half years time I'm looking through the front windshield, not looking through the rear vision mirror. I think we had great success. We took two athletes from our group to Tokyo. Both those athletes stepped up on the podium as individuals, both Emma and Emily Seabock. That's great but it's ancient history to me. So I'm just firmly fixated on two and a half years trying to get people on the team and then once we're on the team trying to get world class improvement from them when they get to the major benchmark so that's all I'm focusing on at the moment. There's so many different avenues that you can improve. This is what I tell all the swimmers in our group. It's skill development. So in swimming the skills are starts, turns and finishes. It's technical improvement, making their strokes more efficient. Speed gains, getting them faster, more enduring, improving on their endurance, improving their attitude. There's a whole host of different things. I've got a lot of older athletes in my program, 26, 27, 28, 29. So to me the recovery is the important thing with those athletes. Like each of them have got a different focus that they've got to work on. I think they've all got strengths and weaknesses and they've got to try and maintain their strengths or slightly improve their strengths but really look at their weaknesses. I think it's the

good athlete that can take the feedback with the weakness and they can work on that information. They're getting a better weakness and make it better. One of our sports scientists gave me an interesting statistic. She heard her talk once and she said, relating to tennis, she said the top 50 players in the world know what they need to do to improve and they actually action that. That's why they keep moving up that top 50 and the bottom 50 or the second 50 of the 100, they know what they need to do to improve but they don't do anything about it. They just sit on it. It's too hard or too difficult and they remain in that bottom 50. They even progress and work down outside the top 100. I think that's a really interesting statistic to me and it's one of the ones I use with our simmers. It's one thing knowing what you've got to do to get improvement but if you've got a start that's not world class, you've got to be staying behind after training, doing half a dozen extra starts every day. Nine sessions a week, that's 54 extra starts that you're doing. One session every week and over the course of six months it's thousands of starts so for you to improve you've got to be prepared to do the extra and go the extra mile to get that improvement. It's not going to just happen. One of the things I say to my simmers, I haven't got a pocket of fairy dust that I can just sprinkle the fairy dust over the top of your head. You've got to be willing to do

the extra little bit to try and gain improvement and it's the people in my group that I've had success with luckily enough over the last 20 years of coaching. They're prepared to do the extra. Stephanie Rice was a classic for that. We used to do dry land for about 30 minutes before core works and medicine ball work for 30 minutes before training. She'd hop in then and do six to seven kilometres and during the swim down, this is before Beijing when she was very successful, during the swim down she'd say Baoli can you stick around for an extra 15 to 20 minutes of extra medicine ball at the end? I said yeah, sure. This is about two months out of Beijing and I'd be there with the medicine ball with her and we'd be going, going and I'd look at my watch and it was ticking over to an hour of extra medicine ball and I had to say step, that's it. Can I just do a little bit? No, that's it. So it was me not telling her to do the extra. It was done with her own volition and then I'd have to be pulling it back and saying hey, hey, that's enough. And I think they're the people ultimately who are successful. They're driven. They're very self, self driven with things. So you've got to be very careful of those athletes because sometimes they can take it too far but that unbridled enthusiasm is something that you've got to try and harness as a coach. So you know you're fortunate I've been very fortunate with the athletes that I've coached. They've been very

goal driven and really wanted to do it. There's very little of me pulling them by the ear to get them to where they wanted to go to. They were you know, they had as much enthusiasm and excitement about being successful as I did. Wow, that's amazing. Finally, I'd like to touch on your mentors along the way. You mentioned a few before. What pieces of information and what things, how did they change the way you approach coaching? Well I think I've been lucky enough to have some very good coaches when I was swimming. I was a former swimmer and Bill Sweetenham was one of my coaches. Laurie Lawrence was one of my coaches. Dennis Pursley, he was a famous American coach, was one of my coaches and I think I learnt quite a bit off those three coaches and I think I learnt what not to do and maybe some things that what not to do. I've got things that I do wrong as well. I know I make mistakes all the time but it's having that ability to be able to learn from those areas that you make and try and make the adjustments in the season that you're currently working through. The two coaches I had it was very much a hard working environment like Laurie and Bill. Both very, very tough, very, very hard. In some cases too much so but I think you can't deny the success they had. They both coached Olympic gold medalists. Now we know it's done differently. We know that the technique is such an important

driver of performance shifting so a lot of video analysis and that sort of stuff wasn't really looked at back in those days and there was probably a little bit too much volume back in those days. It's more race specific stuff but I think the basic cornerstone of what they tried to instill in the athletes that they had was the athletes that came back to the John Wooden industriousness like them understanding, as I understand, to perform well at that very, very high level Olympic level. You're going to be prepared to do what other people aren't prepared to do. You're going to take the less trodden path to gain success and I think being able to absorb work, not being over the top with it but being able to absorb work so they're the fittest, they're the fastest, they're the most skilled, they're the most technically most technically gifted athletes that are racing at world level and you put all of those pieces of the puzzle together. A great attitude, great commitment to what they're doing and you put all those pieces of the puzzle together and you come up with a beautiful picture. But if you're missing one or two pieces of the puzzle, you'll never have the puzzle sold. You'll never get the clear picture. There's been a lot of athletes that I've had over the years that have had super talent but just haven't had that 12 month commitment to the job at hand and they were never able to realise

the talent that they had. I've had many not so talented swimmers that have stood up on podiums at Olympic level, not through talent but through sheer hard work. So I think it's that combination of being talented but having that will to want to work really, really hard, out skill out work other people and you're putting yourself there's no guarantee for success if you want to guarantee you go out and buy a toaster. That's one of the sayings I have in the squad as well. All you can do is try and set yourself up for success and then on the day under the bright spotlight of a meat like the Olympic Games you're going to be able to keep your nerve, you're going to be able to keep relaxed, you've got to have that self-belief and you're going to be able to stand tall and deliver when it counts. That's what we try and set up in training. That's the cornerstone of what we do is in training. There's the standard of your competition, that's the standard of the demand from a physiological sense and what I try and do in training two or three or four times a week is the demand that I'm after is higher than the demand of the race and seeing how the athletes respond, you can't train them that way every day of the week but two, three, four times a week the demand of the training session far away is the demand of the race and I watch how the athletes respond to what I'm giving them. Some take it on

board really, really well and others crumble under that really tough spotlight. Failure isn't fatal like I think Emma wobbled in 2016 in Rio, she swam quite well but she wasn't happy with what she did and she made the necessary adjustments under that five year period and she was the best prepared Emma McKean she could have been when she lined up in Tokyo. So she had 13 races over eight days that were all world class and she did it race after race after race. There was a couple of races there, she had 20, 25 minutes between events and we're not talking about racing on the weekend at the Gold Coast Championships, we're talking about the Olympics. So there were people that she was lining up against that didn't have that demand and they chose one over the other, she chose to do both and stood up and delivered so the training she did reflected the level that she got to in Tokyo so it's been nice to be part of her little journey along the way and hopefully we can go one better with her again in Paris once it comes around. Well it's been fantastic Michael to catch up with you and also to listen to you speak hopefully our coaches have had the opportunity to take in a little bit of that and process it and we might see you on the call tomorrow. Thank you again for your time Michael. No problem, happy to help.
